availability.body: Instead of searching the board, say when you have time: the whole festival, the same hours every day, or a few single dates. Pick one, the grid below changes to match, then save. Organisers see it while they plan, so you stop being asked about the mornings you were never free anyway.
availability.title: Or let the shifts find you

bookIt.body: No form, no approval, no waiting to hear back. One press and the block turns green for you, and the count goes up for everybody else. If something comes up, the same press hands it back. Try it if you like — the tour carries on either way.
bookIt.title: Taking it is one press

finish.body: Jobs get cut into shifts, you take the ones that suit you, and your availability covers the rest. The buttons here take you straight to the jobs and to your own shifts. Have a proper look around — the demo is yours for as long as it lasts.
finish.title: That is all there is to it

jobRow.body: On the left is the job itself: what it is called, where it happens, how many places are still free. The rest of the row is the same job spread across the days of the festival, and every small block in it is one shift. One look down the page shows you where people are still missing.
jobRow.title: One row, one job

jobsIntro.body: A job is something that has to be covered over a stretch of time: a welcome desk all weekend, a café counter on the Saturday. Nobody signs up for a whole job — it gets cut into shifts, and a shift is what you take. This screen shows you both at once.
jobsIntro.title: Jobs, and the shifts in them

myBookings.body: Past and upcoming together, each with the time, the place and the people you are on it with — which is what you actually want on the morning of. This is also where you hand a shift back if something changes. Which leaves one question: how do you find the shifts that suit you?
myBookings.title: Everything you said yes to

nextShift.body: You are already signed up for a few shifts, and the next one always sits at the top: when it starts, where to go, and who else will be there. For most helpers that is the one thing they come to this page to check. Where those shifts come from is the next screen.
nextShift.title: What you are already down for

openChip.body: One block is one shift: the start time on top, and under it the places taken out of the places needed. This one still has room. Pale blocks are full, green ones are yours — that is how you read a whole weekend without opening anything. Press below and I will open this one for you.
openChip.title: A shift with room in it

shiftRoster.body: A shift is not an empty slot, it is a small group with a place left in it. The list is the people who have said yes, and the blank line is the place still going spare. Seeing that others are already in usually settles the question. Where to go and what to bring are right above.
shiftRoster.title: Who is already on it

attention.body: Riverside Summer Festival is half staffed, and this is the part that needs you now: shifts nobody has taken, shifts still short of a pair of hands, and anyone waiting to be let in. Every line is a count and a link at once, so it is a to-do list rather than a status board. When nothing needs doing, the panel is not there at all.
attention.title: What needs you right now

finish.body: Describe a job once, let wirksam cut it into shifts, keep an eye on the thin ones, and read afterwards how it went. Everything you have seen works exactly as it would in a real event — and the person at the door is still waiting. Have a proper look around; the demo is yours for as long as it lasts.
finish.title: That is the whole loop

formIntro.body: Creating a job is this one page, folded into five sections: what the job is, which event it belongs to, which days it runs, how each day is cut up, and a preview. The first two are filled in already so the rest has something to work with, and I will open the others one at a time. Nothing is saved until you say so.
formIntro.title: One form, one job

generateShifts.body: The daily window, how long one shift should run, and how many people it needs. From those three, every shift on every day you picked is worked out, down to the odd half hour left at the end. Change the shift length and watch the count in the preview move. This is the step that saves you typing forty rows by hand.
generateShifts.title: This is where shifts come from

jobRow.body: A job is something that has to be covered over a stretch of time: a welcome desk all weekend, a café counter on the Saturday. You describe it once, on the left of this row. The rest is wirksam's work — the same job cut into single shifts, day by day.
jobRow.title: One row, one job

people.body: Each row is somebody who can see the schedule, and the role beside the name says what they may do with it: members take shifts, admins plan as well, and whoever owns the event can hand it on. Above is the person the dashboard mentioned, still waiting to be let in — accept, and they can start taking shifts straight away. The invitation card below you can only look at: the demo sends no email.
people.title: The people in your event

reporting.body: How much of the schedule filled, the hours people gave, who took on the most, and which times of day were hardest to cover. Beside it is a spreadsheet export for anyone who would rather do their own arithmetic. Useful in the week afterwards, and more useful still when you plan next year's.
reporting.title: How it actually went

shiftPreview.body: Every shift your settings would produce, counted here and listed below, before a single one exists. Tap one to leave it out — the Sunday morning nobody works. Fixing a two-hour block that should have been one costs nothing now, and a great deal once forty people have booked into it. Saving is the button at the bottom; that one is yours.
shiftPreview.title: Check before you save

staffing.body: Each block carries the places taken over the places needed, so a whole weekend's staffing is one look down the page. This one is still short of people; the pale ones are done. That is your list for the week before, and volunteers are looking at exactly the same board. Next comes the form all of this came out of.
staffing.title: Reading the schedule at a glance

taskDates.body: A single day, a run of days, or a few dates scattered across the event — the last one is what a festival with gaps in it really looks like. A short run is picked already, inside the event's own window, which is why the calendar offers you nothing outside it. Everything you set after this applies to each of those days.
taskDates.next: How the day is cut up
taskDates.title: Which days it runs
